text: PostgreSQL does not check for deadlock on every lock: a waiting transaction first sleeps for deadlock_timeout (default 1 second), and only then runs the relatively expensive deadlock check.
why: Explains when detection actually runs and why a deadlocked statement can hang about a second.

text: InnoDB picks the victim by size: it 'tries to pick small transactions to roll back', measured by rows inserted, updated or deleted. The victim gets ERROR 1213 and its whole transaction is rolled back; the application should retry the entire transaction.
why: Tells the reader who gets killed and what the code must do.

text: Oracle breaks a deadlock by rolling back only one statement (of the transaction that detects it), not the whole transaction; the application should then roll back explicitly or retry.
why: Shows victim handling differs across the three databases named.

text: The standard defence: make every code path acquire locks on multiple rows in the same order (for example, ascending primary key). Two transactions that lock rows in the same order cannot form a cycle.
why: Turns 'arrange your statements' into a concrete rule.

text: Under MVCC an exclusive row lock does not block ordinary SELECTs: they read the last committed version. Only other writers and locking reads (FOR SHARE / FOR UPDATE) wait.
why: Corrects the 'not even read' wording.

text: Lock upgrade is a classic deadlock source: if two transactions both hold a shared lock on a row and both then try to update it, each waits for the other's S lock, and InnoDB rolls one back. MySQL's manual uses this as its deadlock example.
why: Warns about the hidden cost of FOR SHARE followed by UPDATE.

text: SKIP LOCKED returns 'an inconsistent view of the data', so both MySQL and PostgreSQL say it is not for general transactional work. It is meant for queue-like tables where any free row will do, like job queues or seat/coupon pools.
why: Sets the boundary of when SKIP LOCKED is safe.

text: In MySQL, SELECT ... FOR SHARE (8.0+) replaces the older SELECT ... LOCK IN SHARE MODE, which still works. Only FOR SHARE supports NOWAIT and SKIP LOCKED.
why: Readers will meet the old syntax in existing code.

text: Real defaults: InnoDB waits innodb_lock_wait_timeout = 50 seconds for a row lock; PostgreSQL's lock_timeout defaults to 0, which means wait indefinitely unless you set it.
why: Gives the actual numbers behind 'say 10 seconds'.

text: After a lock wait timeout, MySQL rolls back only the waiting statement, not the whole transaction (unless --innodb-rollback-on-timeout is set). The transaction stays open and still holds its earlier locks, so the code should roll back or retry.
why: A common source of lingering locks after timeouts.

text: In PostgreSQL at READ COMMITTED, a waiter re-evaluates its WHERE clause against the updated version of the row and skips it if it no longer matches. At REPEATABLE READ the waiter instead fails with 'could not serialize access due to concurrent update' and must retry.
why: Shows approach 4's behaviour depends on isolation level.

text: Indexes matter for locking: in InnoDB a locking read or UPDATE locks every index record it scans, whatever the WHERE clause says. Without a suitable index (for example on trip_id, user_id) it may lock every row of the table.
why: Practical caveat when copying the demo's FOR UPDATE query.

text: Which waiter gets a contended InnoDB lock is decided by Contention-Aware Transaction Scheduling (CATS). The transaction blocking the most others goes first; ties go to the longest-waiting transaction.
why: Backs up 'whichever is scheduled first' with the actual rule.

text: A single 'UPDATE ... SET count = count + 1 WHERE id = ?' does not lose updates: each UPDATE locks the row and a concurrent updater waits, then works on the updated version. Lost updates come from reading the value in the application and writing it back.
why: Separates the safe SQL form from the unsafe read-modify-write.

text: In MySQL's default REPEATABLE READ, all plain SELECTs in a transaction see the snapshot taken at its first read. A transaction that has already read will not see later commits until it commits and starts again.
why: Qualifies 'anyone who reads after a commit sees it'.

text: PostgreSQL has four row-lock strengths: FOR UPDATE, FOR NO KEY UPDATE, FOR SHARE and FOR KEY SHARE. Weaker modes let, for example, foreign-key checks proceed while non-key columns are updated.
why: Shows S/X is the basic model, not the full set.

text: On very high-concurrency InnoDB systems, deadlock detection itself can slow things down when many threads wait on the same lock. MySQL lets you disable it (innodb_deadlock_detect=OFF) and rely on innodb_lock_wait_timeout instead.
why: Real-world cost of the detection the teacher describes.

text: In PostgreSQL any error, including a NOWAIT lock failure, puts the whole transaction block into an aborted state. Only ROLLBACK, or ROLLBACK TO a savepoint taken before the failing statement, recovers it.
why: Explains what 'the transaction kills itself' means in PostgreSQL.

text: PostgreSQL keeps no in-memory list of locked rows: it marks the lock in the row itself, so SELECT FOR UPDATE can cause disk writes. As a result there is no limit on how many rows can be locked at once.
why: Corrects 'not at disk level at all' for one major engine.

text: PostgreSQL warns that at READ COMMITTED a SELECT with ORDER BY and a locking clause can return rows out of order: it sorts first, then may block while locking. With LIMIT, locking stops once enough rows have been returned.
why: Caveat for the ORDER BY id LIMIT 1 FOR UPDATE pattern.
